schools.summary: Gill gives four reasons for the register — Esau was Isaac's son, whose burial has just been told; his descendants are noticed so often later that this genealogy illustrates those places; the promise to Abraham and the oracle to Rebekah about two nations are seen taking effect; and so is Isaac's blessing on this son — and adds a fifth from Maimonides which he thinks the principal one, that Amalek lay under an express sentence of destruction, so the rest of the family had to be described particularly lest they perish with him. Calvin turns the catalogue into a comment on its worth: Esau was an alien from the Church, yet as Isaac's son he had a temporal blessing, and Moses celebrates his race in a commemoration resembling an honourable burial. The precedence was a bubble under the figure of this world, and since no condition lasts outside the kingdom of God the pomp goes off like a scene shifted on a stage; the Spirit, having shown that Isaac's prophecy was not empty, draws our eyes away as though casting a veil, that we may attend to the race of Jacob. On the three wives Calvin refuses to let a good outcome excuse the practice — polygamy is not approved, nor impure lust; what deserves admiration is a goodness that gave a good issue to evil beginnings, against the order of nature.

Henry hears a reproach in the surname, which keeps up the memory of the birthright sold for red pottage, and thinks that enough to explain why this family is dismissed so briefly: if men do a wrong thing they must thank themselves when it is remembered against them long afterwards. Three wives, he notes, and by all three only five sons, where many a man has more by one; God often disappoints those who take crooked ways to build a house, though here the promise prevailed. He also weighs the brothers — in outward prosperity the children of the covenant are often behind and those outside the covenant get the start, and it must have tried Israel's faith to hear of the pomp of Edom's kings while they were bond-slaves in Egypt, but men who look for great things from God must wait.

Clarke says the generations are set down so exactly to show how exactly God kept his promise to this son, and that the Horite line is appended because the two families afterwards became blended. Wesley, with Henry, hears the reproach in the name Edom.

Keil and Delitzsch reason from the structure: Esau too had a divine promise, and his tribe's future was woven into the paternal blessing, so its growth into a nation gets a section of its own, standing by the book's plan before the generations of Jacob and subdivided by its own headings; they quote Delitzsch on the brothers shaking hands once more over their father's corpse, their paths thenceforth diverging to meet no more. Ellicott opens with a warning about how to read the section, which abounds in difficulties too often aggravated by commentators determined to make Scripture bend to their notions of what it ought to be rather than accept it as it is. His test case is the list of kings: no prophetical passage but a dry genealogical table, whose plain sense — that when it was written there were kings in Israel — commentators evade in ways painful to read and apt only to harden sceptics. Nor will he call the closing lists interpolations, since completing a genealogy was ordinary and the prophets had authority to add what was needed; he instances the note about Rachel's pillar standing unto this day, and dates those documents to about the time the Books of Samuel were composed.

debates: When the closing lists were written. Ellicott takes the clause about kings in Israel at face value and dates the last two documents to about the time of the Books of Samuel, defending the addition as within prophetic authority; the reading is disputed elsewhere in the chapter.

2.pericope_label: Esau's wives and the sons born in Canaan

schools.summary: Gill notes that these were daughters of Canaan, of the posterity of cursed Canaan — most of them, though not all, one wife coming of Ishmael's family. On the sons he passes on two rabbinic questions: Jerome and the Targum of Jonathan make Eliphaz the friend who visited Job, though Gill thinks that man his grandson, being called the Temanite; and the Korah listed here turns up again among the sons of Eliphaz, where Jarchi takes them for one man and a bastard while Aben Ezra argues for a single Korah, Aholibamah's son, reckoned among Eliphaz's because he lived among them or was reared by Adah after his mother died young.

Clarke lists the changes of name — the Aholibamah here appears earlier as Judith, Adah there as Bashemath, this Bashemath as Mahalath elsewhere — and declines to spend time on them, since they cannot easily be accounted for, are not worth detaining a reader, and the same persons in Scripture often bear different names. On the contradiction between Anah as daughter and as son of Zibeon he sets out the remedies: the Samaritan, Greek and Syriac read son, which Houbigant and Kennicott hold the true text, while others refer daughter to Aholibamah; Clarke prefers the first, which brings every mention into agreement.

Ellicott builds on what Clarke waves away. The double naming he explains by the woman's being a Hittite whose name in her own tongue was neither Adah nor Bashemath, both perhaps endearments formed from it; Aholibamah he separates from Judith altogether, since her grandfather Zibeon is called a Horite further down and the letters for Hivite and Horite differ by a single stroke. From that the order of the list falls into place — Judith childless, Adah first as the first wife who bore sons, Aholibamah third because taken last — and so does the presence of a Horite pedigree in the chapter, Esau having gained ducal rank and friendly terms with part of that people by marrying a duke's daughter. He notes a second textual slip in the Samaritan's Mahalath, which he thinks right though the versions side with the Masoretic text, and closes by dating the migration: Esau kept his home at Hebron for twenty-two years after Jacob's return and only moved to Seir when Isaac died, so that the birthright came to Jacob by Esau's own act. Keil and Delitzsch record only that the names differ from the earlier accounts.

debates: How much the discrepant names matter. Clarke treats the variations as unimportant and common in Scripture; Ellicott makes them the key to the chapter, distinguishing Aholibamah from Judith and reading the whole order of the list from the sequence of the marriages.

schools.summary: Gill marks what the list leaves out — the wives and sons are named, but of the daughters neither names nor number — compares the parting to that of Abraham and Lot, and sorts through explanations of the mountain's name, rejecting Josephus, who derives it from Esau's own shaggy hair, and still more R. Abraham Seba's satyrs and hairy demons, in favour of Seir the Horite or the rugged look of the hill itself, which sets it against the bald Mount Halak nearby; he adds the Targum's Mount Gabla and the district Gobolites, perhaps the Gebal of Scripture, and has Esau drive out the Horites once matters with his brother were amicably settled. Calvin denies that Esau withdrew to make room for Jacob: he was too proud and ferocious ever to seem his brother's inferior, and moved for the advantage he expected, Moses ignoring the man's design to commend the secret providence that drove him into exile — God leading the blind man by the hand lest he settle where his own servant was to be, as the wicked so often do the elect good against their intention. Even the vagueness of the phrase is evidence, Esau departing simply into the country with his plan unsettled until Seir offered itself, going out at a venture.

Clarke takes the withdrawal for dignified conduct of a piece with the rest of Esau's behaviour toward his brother, the two having lived together in Canaan on the friendliest footing since Jacob's return, and Esau leaving the better country to him for a far less fruitful one. Wesley traces the move in stages: Esau had begun settling among his wife's relations before Jacob came back, sent there most likely by Isaac to clear Jacob's way, kept property in Canaan while his father lived, and withdrew for good only after the death — partly because Jacob held the promise, partly because two households thriving at that rate would not both have room. He closes on the theology of it, that God's word takes place whatever opposition is made.

Ellicott gives the Hebrew as into a land away from the face, calls the separation as inevitable and quite ordinary among nomads, since a tribe grows only as far as its district will feed it, and notes that the pressure was worse because both men were sojourners among tribes that claimed the soil — which may itself have pointed Esau toward Seir, where he ranked as a duke in right of Aholibamah. He cites Maimonides for the view that Esau had hunted and perhaps raided there but lacked the strength to seize the country until Isaac's death multiplied his retainers, and describes Idumea: a limestone chain veined with basalt running from the south end of the Dead Sea to the Gulf of Elath, much of it too stony to bear anything and the rest fertile in figs and pomegranates rather than corn, with summers cooled by winds and cold winters, its border only fifty or sixty miles from Hebron.

debates: Whether Esau's withdrawal was generous. Clarke reads it as dignified conduct toward his brother; Calvin denies any such intention, holding Esau too proud to seem Jacob's inferior and attributing the move to present advantage and to a providence working against the man's own design.
themes: riches too great to dwell together

9.pericope_label: The generations of Esau in Seir

schools.summary: Gill gives the posterity of Esau, his children and grandchildren, and identifies Teman, the firstborn of Eliphaz, as the source of the name of the city of Teman in Idumea, which is why Eliphaz himself is called the Temanite. Calvin takes the second name as pointing forward to the posterity called Idumeans, and thinks Moses styles Esau father of a celebrated and famous people on purpose, to show what God had bestowed on him for his father Isaac's sake; tracing the prophecy into his progeny serves a further end, since if the promise flourished so mightily toward a stranger it must work more powerfully toward the children to whom the adoption belongs. Esau was an obscure man and a sojourner, and could hardly have won such power unopposed — a people of no ignoble name held Mount Seir before him, and Moses says the earlier inhabitants were mighty — so the blessing out of Isaac's mouth must have been confirmed by the event.

Henry fastens on what the register withholds: only names, not history, because it is the church whose records Moses keeps; the elders who lived by faith obtained the good report, and it is Sion that produces the men of renown, not Seir. The line stops at the third and fourth generation while the pedigree of Israel runs on through every tribe until Canaan was divided and through the royal line until Christ came. On the title he goes further than Wesley: titles of honour have been older outside the church than in it, Esau's sons being dukes while Jacob's were plain shepherds — no argument against Christians using such titles, but a reason not to overvalue anyone for them, since Edomites may be dukes among men while Israelites indeed are made kings and priests to our God. He adds that it is nothing new for the men of this world to have their bellies filled with hidden treasure.

Wesley says the same things in nearly the same words — only names and no history, the line stopping at the third and fourth generation, the dukes taken for military commanders since Esau's family lived by the sword, the dukedoms large households of children and servants, and God's promise to Jacob beginning to work late, lasting longer, and having its complete accomplishment in the spiritual Israel.

Ellicott points out that the Hebrew says father of Edom, and that since Esau was himself the man Edom the word must here mean the country he colonised. Keil and Delitzsch attend to the word behind duke: aluphim was the distinguishing title of the Edomite and Horite phylarchs, applied to Jewish heads of tribes only incidentally and late, in Zechariah, and probably derived from the word for a thousand, which stands elsewhere for families.

outliers: Wesley's note here is an abridgement of Henry's, following it point by point and often word for word; the two are treated as one position rather than as independent agreement.

12.pericope_label: Timna, Amalek and the sons of Reuel

schools.summary: Gill reports that Timna was sister to Lotan, the eldest son of Seir the Horite, and lays out two rabbinic attempts to reconcile her with the Timna among the sons of Eliphaz and the duke of that name later — Gerundinsis having the concubine bear Amalek, conceive again and die in childbirth, the father naming the second child after her; Jarchi making Timna the daughter of Eliphaz by Lotan's mother, and afterwards his concubine, so that she was at once his daughter and his concubine. Of the remaining names he says only that Reuel was another son of Esau with four sons of his own.

Clarke takes the relationship as the historical hinge: Timna's being Lotan's sister shows how the family of Esau and the Horites came to be intermixed, and that intermixture later gave Esau's sons their pretext for seizing the land and driving out its old inhabitants. Of Amalek he says what the rest of Scripture says — father of the Amalekites, afterwards bitter enemies of the Jews, a people God commanded to be exterminated outright.

Ellicott will not have the descent so simple. Balaam calls Amalek the beginning of nations, a phrase implying precedence and nobility, and the race held the whole country from Shur on the border of Egypt to Havilah in Arabia Felix; a people of that standing can hardly have sprung from the concubine of Eliphaz. His solution is a fusion — some Horites absorbed into the Amalekites, as the Kenezites under Caleb were absorbed into Judah — and he makes this Amalek the founder only of the Amalekites whom the Simeonites afterwards smote in Mount Seir, since a duke's descendants would hold a district of their own, its chiefs Semites of Esau's line and its people a blend of Horite and Amalekite. Their absence from the table of nations he thinks no difficulty: whatever Balaam made of them, Israel never regarded them as a nation, only as a hateful horde of plunderers.

debates: Whether the Amalekite nation descends from this Amalek. Clarke takes him straight as father of the Amalekites; Ellicott denies that so widespread and ancient a race can have sprung from a concubine of Eliphaz, and makes him founder only of the Amalekites settled in Seir.
themes: a horde and not a nation

15.pericope_label: The dukes of the sons of Esau

schools.summary: Gill reports Ben Melech's distinction that a king is crowned and a duke is not, but prefers Jarchi's reading of the word as head of a family, which fits the context. On the disputed name he declines to cut: he notes its omission in the Samaritan and the absence of any such son from the earlier list, then offers Gerundinsis's identification of this Korah with the Timna reckoned among Eliphaz's sons, or else supposes a grandson of Eliphaz.

Clarke goes at the title through the languages — duke is the Latin dux, a captain or leader, and the Hebrew alluph means the same; since the word also stands for a thousand, the alluphey were probably so called from commanding a thousand men, like the chiliarchs among the Greeks and the centurions among the Romans. He notes that this ducal government was the earliest form among the Idumeans and counts fourteen dukes to Esau, seven from Adah, four from Bashemath and three from Aholibamah. On the disputed name he states Dr Kennicott's case at length: Eliphaz had six sons, none of them Korah, and Korah was Esau's own son by Aholibamah, so a copyist inserted the name here, from which insertion both the Samaritan text and version are free — everything considered, Clarke inclines to think the words were never in the text.

Ellicott makes the office territorial rather than military. Alluph means a tribal prince, and eleph, a thousand, was used much as our own word hundred once was for a division of country — a district large enough to hold a thousand grown men, where the Saxon hundred held a hundred homesteads — each prince governing one such district as a possession for himself and his seed. He agrees in a sentence that the Samaritan rightly omits the disputed name, and finds a reason for the shape of the list: Aholibamah's three sons are themselves dukes where the other wives are represented only by grandsons, probably because she came of the ruling family of Seir and her sons took command of Horite districts in her right. Keil and Delitzsch look ahead to the people already in the land — the Horite is the dweller in caves, the Greek rendering it troglodyte, and caves abound in the mountains of Edom; once independent, they were afterwards in part exterminated and in part subjugated.

debates: Whether duke Korah belongs in the list. Clarke, following Kennicott, and Ellicott both treat it as a copyist's insertion absent from the Samaritan; Gill keeps it, offering instead an identification with the Timna among Eliphaz's sons, or a grandson of that name.

20.pericope_label: Seir the Horite and his sons

schools.summary: Gill notes the Targum's added word — these inhabited the land before it belonged to Esau's posterity — and that the Horites were there as far back as Abraham's day, named from living underground in holes and caves, the people the Greeks call Trogloditae; Jarchi reports from the Rabbins that they were expert judges of ground and knew what would carry olives and what vines. He gives two reasons for the insertion, to show who held the country before Esau's sons succeeded them and because of the intermarriages that eased the transfer, and counts the sons — Dishon, Ezer and Dishan making seven with the four already named.

Henry takes the intermarriage as an indictment: the Horite genealogy stands in the middle of the Edomite one not merely to light up the story but as a standing reproach to the Edomites for marrying into that stock, by which they probably learned their ways and corrupted themselves. Esau had sold his birthright, lost his blessing and allied himself with the Hittites, so his posterity and the sons of Seir are reckoned together — men who treacherously desert God's church are justly numbered with those who were never in it, and apostate Edomites stand on the same ground as accursed Horites. He then singles out Anah, who fed his father's asses and is nevertheless called a duke, for two kinder morals: those who expect to rise high should begin low, and an honourable descent should keep no man from honest work, nor mean work hinder his advancement.

Clarke says these were the original inhabitants of what was called the land of the Horites and afterwards of the Idumeans once Esau's descendants had driven them out, and observes that Horites and Edomites were mixed together in one land, citing Calmet's remark that setting this verse beside the later list shows princes of Seir both in Seir and in Edom, which obliges us to treat the two lines as contemporary. Wesley repeats Henry's indictment and his morals on Anah, adding that the man was ingenious and successful as well as industrious.

Ellicott gives his own pair of reasons for the insertion: the list contains Aholibamah's pedigree, but chiefly the Horites were in time fused with the descendants of Esau and together formed the Edomites. He also disentangles a name — the Timna here is sister to Lotan and so to Zibeon, the grandfather of Esau's wife, whereas the Timna of the earlier verse was concubine to Esau's grandson and four generations her junior. Keil and Delitzsch render the closing formula flatly, the princes of the Horites according to their princes.

outliers: Henry and Wesley turn a genealogical aside into two contrary lessons in the same breath — the Edomites condemned for marrying Horites, and a Horite duke praised for having herded his father's asses.

24.pericope_label: Anah and the finding in the wilderness

schools.summary: Gill keeps to the frame of the list, noting only that Zibeon was Seir's third son. Calvin reads the verse as the mule-translation has it and turns it into a reproof: mules are the adulterous offspring of horse and ass, and Anah is named as the author of the connection, but that is no praise of his industry, since God did not distinguish the kinds of animals from the beginning for nothing. The vanity of the flesh forever pushes the children of this world to busy themselves with superfluous things, and Moses marks an unnatural pursuit in a man not content with a great stock unless he could add a degenerate race got by unnatural coupling — there being more moderation among brutes in keeping the law of their nature than among men, who invent vicious mixtures.

Clarke sets out the whole wreckage of opinion on the disputed word. Jerome, who renders it warm springs, said there were as many opinions as commentators; the Greek turns it into what looks like a man's name, the Syriac gives waters, Onkelos giants, the Samaritan text and version the Emim, and the Targum of Jonathan ben Uzziel has Anah put the onager to the tame ass and in time find mules bred between them, an account Kimchi and Jarchi follow. Against these he sets Bochart's four arguments for the Emim — that the verb means lighting upon rather than inventing, that mules bear another name in Scripture, that Anah pastured asses and not horses, and that no mule is mentioned in Palestine before David — with Gusset returning to mules and Wagenseil supposing a plant. The reader, Clarke says, may take whichever opinion he likes best or invent one of his own; his own is that mules were unknown before Anah, and he adds a conjecture that the Enetae, whom Homer makes famous for wild mules, may have taken their fabulous descent from this same man. Wesley takes the clause as a compliment: Anah was industrious and ingenious besides, and successful, and those diligent in their business sometimes find greater advantages than they looked for.

Ellicott decides the question the other way and thinks it settled. Mules is the traditional Jewish rendering, but horses were unknown in Palestine at this date, so Anah cannot have discovered how to cross them with asses; and Jerome records that in Punic, a language akin to Hebrew, the word means hot springs — a translation now generally adopted. He points to Lange's list of hot springs in the Edomite country and picks out those of Calirrhoe, the stream of beauty, in the Wady Zerka Maion.

debates: What Anah found. Clarke surveys the versions and settles for mules, unknown before his time; Ellicott argues that horses were not yet in Palestine and adopts Jerome's Punic sense of hot springs, naming Calirrhoe; Calvin and Wesley both read mules but draw opposite morals from the discovery.
outliers: Clarke ends his survey by inviting the reader to choose whichever opinion he likes best, or invent one for himself — and then offers his own conjecture that Homer's mule-breeding Enetae took their fabulous descent from this Anah.

schools.summary: Gill reaches the elective reading through Bishop Cumberland, who took these for Horite kings setting up a monarchy after their defeat by Chedorlaomer, to be better secured against another such disaster, and cites Maimonides for the observation that not one of them was an Edomite. Calvin puts the lesson in a figure: reprobates are lifted suddenly that they may fall at once, like the herb on the housetop, rootless, quick to spring and quicker to wither. Both sons of Isaac were promised kings, and Idumea began first, so that Israel looked the poorer — but time taught how much better it is to creep along the ground striking root deep than to hold a moment's extravagant pre-eminence.

Henry credits the elective arrangement to bishop Patrick and takes the sequence as doctrine. God had lately promised Jacob that kings should come of his loins, and Esau's blood turns royal long before any of Jacob's, for in outward prosperity the children of the covenant are often cast behind; the triumphing of the wicked is quick but short, soon ripe and as soon rotten, while the products of the promise are slow but sure. He reads the later return to dukes as a demotion — either the Edomites copied the Horite form or providence reduced them to it for refusing Israel a road through their country — and adds that when power is abused it is just with God to weaken it by splitting it into channels, sin bringing Edom from kings to dukes, from crowns to coronets.

Clarke is unsettled by the clause about Israel's kings and thinks the whole passage was transferred here out of Chronicles, since Moses can hardly have written it; he offers a mechanism, the succession noted early in the margin of some authentic copy and taken into the text by a later transcriber who mistook a marginal entry for a repaired omission, as glosses and restorations alike passed into the Vulgate and Septuagint and into a fourteenth-century English Bible lying before him. He knows the alternative, that king may mean any settled government by chiefs, dukes or judges, and does not find it satisfactory; he reckons Esau had eight kings after his dukes, reigning while Israel was afflicted in Egypt. Wesley follows Henry on the elective throne and the demotion to dukes.

Keil and Delitzsch reason from the list itself: the eight follow one another, none coming to the throne until his predecessor is dead, yet no son succeeds his father, every man belongs to a different family and town, and of the last the notice that he died is missing — so the sovereignty was elective, the kings chosen by the phylarchs and reigning alongside them, since Moses treats with a king of Edom about passage through the land while his own song makes the princes tremble. Ellicott fills in the period between: the song at the sea still knows dukes of Edom, and by the time Israel reached the borders Edom had a king, so these were probably petty monarchs thrown up in different quarters during a long civil war in which the Horites were as thoroughly beaten as the Canaanites afterwards under Saul and Solomon, the Horite dukes of Seir's line vanishing altogether.

debates: Whether Moses wrote the list of kings. Clarke holds it was transferred from Chronicles by way of a marginal note, and rejects the softening reading of king as any settled government; Henry and Wesley take the clause at face value as dating the kings before Moses; Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott treat the list as evidence about Edomite institutions without raising the question here.

schools.summary: Gill guards the first king from two men he is not — Balak of Moab, whom the Greek spelling suggests, and the Balaam some in Aben Ezra proposed, who lived ages later — and says that beyond his being the first of these Horite kings, and a date from Bedford, we know no more than the verse tells us, nor how long he reigned, nor whether he left sons, since none followed him. Through the rest of the list his contribution is a chronology taken from Bedford, a date of death for each king in turn, with the note that one of them died better than forty years after the death of Abraham.

Clarke reports the old identification of the second king with Job, and of Eliphaz with Job's friend, and refuses it: there is no proper proof and many reasons against. He passes on Bishop Cumberland's conjecture that the Midian smitten in the field of Moab was Midian the son of Abraham by Keturah, killed before he was a hundred and nine, and that Moses recorded the stroke because it fell on an ancestor of his own father-in-law Jethro.

Ellicott dismisses the identification with Job in a line, noting that the Greek translators made it on no probable grounds, and takes the opposite lesson from the silence about the Midianite victory: every memory of the exploit has perished, and the Bible's complete silence about all these kings suggests they belong to a period earlier than the time when Israel began keeping careful record. He reads Rehoboth by the river as Rehoboth-of-the-river, distinguished from the other Rehoboth, and observes that if the Euphrates is meant the town lay outside Edomite ground and its king probably held Idumea by conquest; the last name he would correct to Hadad, the form of the Samaritan text and of the Hebrew in Chronicles, the two letters being repeatedly confused — and this, he reminds us, is the king who seems to have been still living when the catalogue was drawn up.

debates: Whether Jobab is the Job of the book of afflictions. The Greek translators made the identification and many have followed it, taking Eliphaz for Job's friend; Clarke rejects it as unproved and against many reasons, and Ellicott as resting on no probable grounds.
themes: Bela and the names he is not

40.pericope_label: The dukes according to their places

schools.summary: Gill keeps the two races of dukes apart: after the monarchy ceased the government reverted to dukes, the earlier drawn partly from Seir's line and partly from Esau's and holding office side by side rather than in succession. He notices which names are missing from that earlier list — neither Esau himself nor his sons by the two first wives are called dukes, only the three sons of the last wife, all the rest being grandsons — and takes that as light on when the dukedoms began, guessing that the joint weight of the two intermarried houses ended the regal power. He locates what names he can out of Jerome: Oolibama a city of the princes of Edom, Elath a country of theirs and a city of Esau ten miles east of Petra, Phinon between Petra and Zoar, Teman a village five miles from Petra with a Roman garrison in Jerome's day, and Mabsar the large village Mabsara in Gabalena belonging to Petra.

Clarke limits their authority: they did not govern the whole Idumean nation but were chiefs in their own families and places, the districts they ruled and gave their names to; and he passes on Calmet's opinion that the men named here were the dukes in office when Israel came out of Egypt.

Ellicott reads the list as a map. It is territorial — which does not mean the men were fictions, but that Edom finally settled into eleven thousands called after these chieftains, as the names of Jacob's sons became the names of districts in Canaan. What strikes him is the scale of the change: not one Horite duke has left his name on any division of the country, and of the thirteen tribal princes at first only Teman and Kenaz still carry the names of Esau's sons. Of the other nine nothing is known, though they probably rose during the troubled years when one king after another seized the crown and was displaced — many such men appeared, and these are the ones who consolidated power enough to leave a name. He adds a caution about the word family, which in Hebrew means a larger division of a tribe, subdivided into fathers' houses and again into households, and would render the closing word not habitations but settlements. Keil and Delitzsch let the list stand as it is.

Gill reports from Jerome that Magdiel lay in Gabalena, once held by the dukes of Edom, and from the Targum of Jonathan that the duke took his name from his city, a strong migdal or tower; then Jarchi's gloss — this is Rome — and the saying among Jewish writers that Esau had a hundred provinces from Seir to Magdiel. The closing formula he takes as a claim of full title: the earlier dukes were dukes in the land of Edom, sojourners there, or at least not the only dukes there, men of Seir's race holding rank beside them, whereas these later ones, having driven the Horites out, were sole possessors and lords — and so it stood while Israel's posterity were sojourners in a strange land.

Clarke closes Esau's history and then defends him, nothing more of the man appearing in the Pentateuch and he a fixture in polemic divinity. Apart from selling the birthright and threatening his brother the record is clean, hunger and Jacob's hard bargain accounting for the first and the second never being attempted though he had every means. He quotes Shuckford at length — Esau plain, generous and honest, all humanity at the meeting, no resentment at Jacob's settling near his father, no difficulty at Isaac's death about leaving Canaan; the sentence against him passed before the children had done good or evil; the hatred bringing no punishment, since his posterity held a land God assigned them and Israel was strictly warned not to invade it; all he lost being the inheritance of the promise, which Lot and Job never had either; and profane marking not a wicked man but one who set no due value on the priest's office. Clarke's own summary is that the Messiah had to come through one family, from which it does not follow that the chosen were all saved and the others lost. He ends by defending the genealogies themselves as proof that the prophecies naming one family were fulfilled, and as an argument the Jews cannot now answer, the registers having perished with Jerusalem so that no one can trace himself to David. Wesley makes the contrast the moral of the whole register: Israel in the house of bondage with Canaan only promised, the Edomites in their own habitations with Seir in possession — the children of this world having all in hand and nothing in hope, and the children of God often all in hope and next to nothing in hand, so that it is better to have Canaan in promise than mount Seir in possession.

outliers: Clarke devotes the close of the chapter to rehabilitating Esau, quoting Shuckford at length to argue that he was no worse than other men of his age, that the hatred spoken of brought him no punishment, and that he may be hoped for at the last day with Lot and Job.
